statements.claim: The avadhuta watched a moth circle a lamp flame and fall into it, at night, by a lamp in a wayside rest-house, and counted the moth among his teachers.
statements.evidence: The moth-into-flame exemplum is the source's own simile (BP 11.8.6-7: the uncontrolled man falls like the moth into the flame), and the moth is one of the avadhuta's named gurus (BP 11.7.33-34, corpus chain DKS_0505); but the specific witnessed scene (wayside rest-house, night lamp) is dramatized setting not present in the pack.

statements.claim: Bewitched by a woman's beauty — the gold of her ornaments, the fine weave of her clothes — the man not master of his senses falls into blinding darkness, as the moth into the flame.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.6-7: dṛṣṭvā striyaṃ deva-māyāṃ tad-bhāvair ajitendriyaḥ / yoṣid-dhiraṇyābharaṇāmbarādi-dravyeṣu māyā-raciteṣu mūḍhaḥ — seeing woman, the uncontrolled man falls into blinding darkness; the gold ornaments and garments are in the verse.

statements.claim: The wandering teacher was an avadhuta — a brahmin who had put aside home, name and belongings — who walked the forest roads taking lessons from everything he met, with no guru but the world.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain: BP 11.7.24 (avadhūta brahmin wandering fearlessly), 11.7.33-34 (list of his gurus incl. the moth), established in DKS_0505/0506; consistent with this pack.

statements.claim: He learned to read the smallest things — a drop of water, a bent blade of grass, a sparrow's quarrel — each a page of some teaching; nothing was too small to teach him, and nothing too small to destroy a man.
statements.evidence: Generic illustration of the avadhuta's practice of taking gurus from earth, water, creatures etc. (BP 11.7.33, chain DKS_0505-0506); the specific instances are atmospheric, not asserted by this pack.

statements.claim: The moth's lesson was desire: the flame asks nothing, the moth gives everything; so a man who is not master of his senses follows beauty's brightness and falls — and the avadhuta had seen it happen to men he knew.
statements.evidence: The teaching itself is supported (BP 11.8.6-7); 'he had seen it happen to men he knew — sensible men undone by a face' is invented personal history used as connective rhetoric, asserting no sourceable canonical event.

statements.claim: It is not that beauty is false; it is that desire cannot stop at looking — it must draw nearer until the lovely light is the fire that burns.
statements.evidence: Interpretive gloss on the moth simile consistent with the verse's point; not itself a sourceable claim.

statements.claim: The bee taught the other way: the sage gathers the essence from great and small teachings as the bee gathers from flowers, and stores nothing up.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.9 (aṇubhyaś ca mahadbhyaś ca śāstrebhyaḥ kuśalo naraḥ — the wise man [gathers essence] from small and great scriptures) with the bee simile; pack excerpt: 'the sage gathers the essence from great and small teachings, like the bee from flowers, but stores nothing for tomorrow.'

statements.claim: The bee visits many flowers and takes from each only a little, carrying nothing away to hoard; each blossom is left able to bloom again.
statements.evidence: Naturalistic elaboration of the bee simile from the pack excerpt; description of how bees work, not a canonical event claim.

statements.claim: He eats a little at a time, just enough to keep the body alive, and what is begged for the day is used that same day; he never lays it up for the evening or the morning.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.8 (stokaṃ stokaṃ grased grāsaṃ deho varteta yāvatā) and 11.8.10-11 (sāyantanaṃ śvastanaṃ vā na saṅgṛhṇīta bhikṣitam / bhikṣukaḥ).

statements.claim: The avadhuta said he had made himself the bee — tasting sweetness without owning it, listening to great and small teachings without serving any, sleeping with empty hands, free of the need that makes men hold on.
statements.evidence: First-person dramatization of the teaching in 11.8.8-11; consistent but the 'he had made himself the bee' claim is connective.

statements.claim: The moth and the bee together are one complete teaching: the moth shows what appetite costs, the bee what appetite is for.
statements.evidence: Closing synthesis of the two supported lessons; non-factual framing.

notes: Faithful to BP 11.8.6-11. Scene-setting (rest-house, watching the moth, 'men he knew') is dramatized connective narration around the source's similes; no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims. Avadhuta/guru-list identity supported via corpus chain (DKS_0505, BP 11.7).

statements.claim: The elephant — the strongest thing in the forest, able to uproot a tree — is caught by a she-elephant: hunters send the cow out as a decoy and the great male follows her into the clearing where rope and stake wait; he is not conquered but led.
statements.evidence: The pack supports the core image — 'bound like the elephant caught by the she-elephant' (BP 11.8.12) — but the hunters-decoy/rope-and-stake mechanism is a dramatized naturalistic gloss of how such capture happens; the source records no specific capture scene.

statements.claim: If desire can bind an elephant, what will it do to a man; strength counts for nothing against desire — the elephant could have broken every rope and instead stood quietly while it was tied.
statements.evidence: Expansion of the 11.8.12 simile (the ascetic bound like the elephant caught by the she-elephant); rhetorical elaboration, consistent with the pack.

statements.claim: A renunciate should not touch a woman even of wood; the wise do not go near what brings the death of the self.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.12-13: padāpi yuvatīṃ bhikṣur na spṛśed dāravīm api / nādhigacchet striyaṃ prājñaḥ karhicin mṛtyum ātmanaḥ.

statements.claim: The honey-gatherer climbs to the wild hive in the rocks, is swarmed and stung for every comb he takes, and comes down aching and half-blinded carrying honey — which others eat; he keeps only the scars, and climbs again next season.
statements.evidence: Dramatization of the pack's honey-gatherer exemplum ('the wealth painfully hoarded is enjoyed by others, as the honey-gatherer steals the bees' honey'; BP 11.8.14-15: wealth painfully amassed by the greedy is enjoyed by others). Scene details are connective inference.

statements.claim: So it is with wealth painfully hoarded: a man gathers it in sleeplessness and worry and in the end others enjoy it; the sage does not pile up what was gathered in suffering.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.14-15 (na deyaṃ nopabhogyaṃ ca lubdhair yad duḥkha-sañcitam / su-duḥkhopārjitair vittair āśāsānāṃ gṛhāśiṣaḥ) and the pack's honey-gatherer rendering.

statements.claim: The deer — swift and watchful, uncatchable in a run — is caught by song: hunters lure it with a flute and it stops, ears turned to the music, forgetting what kept it safe.
statements.evidence: Pack supports 'the deer is snared by song' (BP 11.8.16-17, where the point is the renunciate not listening to village music/dancing/songs of women); the flute-lure hunting scene is dramatized connective detail.

statements.claim: A wandering renunciate should not listen to the music and dancing of the village, the songs that please the senses; the sweetest sound can be the snare.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.16-17: grāmya-gītaṃ na śṛṇuyād yatir vana-caraḥ kvacit / nṛtya-vāditra-gītāni juṣan grāmyāṇi yoṣitām.

statements.claim: The fish is caught by the mouth and hooked through the tongue; the taste of the bait undoes it.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'the fish, allured by the tongue's bait, meets death on the hook' (BP 11.8.18: jihvayāti-pramāthinyā jano rasa-vimohitaḥ).

statements.claim: Of all the senses the tongue is the hardest to master: a man may close his eyes and stop his ears, but the craving for taste follows him everywhere — a man may refuse cup and plate and still be undone by the memory of a taste.
statements.evidence: The tongue's power to delude is in BP 11.8.18 (ati-pramāthinī, rasa-vimohitaḥ); 'hardest to master' and the closable-eyes/ears and memory-of-taste elaborations are interpretive connective glosses.

statements.claim: The senses are conquered quickly when they are not fed — the secret is to stop feeding them.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.19: indriyāṇi jayanty āśu nirāhārā manīṣiṇaḥ.

statements.claim: It must be all the senses together: a man who has mastered one sense while another rules him is not yet master of anything.
statements.evidence: BP 11.8.20: tāvaj jitendriyo na syād vijitānyendriyaḥ pumān.

statements.claim: The avadhuta walked on past the village music and the markets' sweets, having seen where each road ended — in the rope, in the stings, in the bow, in the hook.
statements.evidence: Closing connective recap of the four exempla; 'in the bow' alludes to the deer's end, not stated in the pack.

notes: Faithful to BP 11.8.12-20 (elephant/wooden-woman, hoarded wealth, village music, tongue, fasting the senses, all-senses-together). All scene mechanics (decoy cow, hive in rocks, flute lure) are connective dramatizations of pack-supported exempla — no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED claims.

statements.claim: The osprey, carrying prey, was mobbed from every side by stronger birds; it let the meat fall, the attackers wheeled away after it, and the osprey flew on free and unhurt.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.1 (sāmiṣaṃ kuraraṃ jaghnur balino 'nye nirāmiṣāḥ — other strong, meatless birds struck the osprey holding prey) and pack index summary ('letting go of prey seized by stronger birds'); the letting-go outcome is the point of the exemplum.

statements.claim: The birds that took the meat were no stronger in the wing than the osprey — only more numerous, and more hungry.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.1 says the attackers WERE the strong ones (balino 'nye nirāmiṣāḥ — 'other strong birds without prey'; standard translations: 'a hawk carrying meat was attacked by stronger hawks'), the pack's index summary says the prey was 'seized by stronger birds', and the story's own opening paragraph says 'the stronger birds came'. The story's later claim that they were only more numerous contradicts the verse, the index, and itself.

statements.claim: The lesson was in the letting go: it was not hunger that endangered the bird but the prize; so it is with a man who grips what he cannot keep.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the exemplum's point (attachment to prey brings the attack; the unattached are unassailed — gitabase on SB 11.9: 'attachment creates misery, but the person who is unattached... is qualified'); framed as connective commentary.

statements.claim: The avadhuta said he had made himself like the osprey: for him there was neither honor nor disgrace, and none of the cares that keep householders wakeful, because he had let them all go.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.2: na me mānāpamānau sto na cintā geha-putriṇām (I have neither honor nor disgrace, nor the anxiety of householders with sons).

statements.claim: Only two beings are free of care — the child, who has nothing and wants nothing, absorbed in its own joy, and the sage; from the child he learned to be glad without possessions.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.3 (dvāv eva cintayā muktau paramānanda āplutau — two alone are free of care, immersed in supreme bliss; the child and the sage, per the pack index 'the child (freedom from care)'); the child-at-play description is connective color.

statements.claim: A maiden, alone in the house husking grain, heard her bangles clink at every stroke, minded the noise as unbecoming, and broke them off one by one until a single bangle remained — and a single bangle makes no sound.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.4-8 (kumārī alone husking rice in private; her two wristlets' clink judged unbecoming (jugupsita); she broke them one by one until one remained — with one there is no sound); pack excerpt: 'a maiden, alone, husking grain, heard her bangles clink and broke them one by one until only one remained, and it was silent.'

statements.claim: So should the sage dwell: alone; where many live together there is quarreling, and even two voices make a noise; strip away what clinks and there is silence.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.9: vāse bahūnāṃ kalaho bhaved vārtā dvayor api (in the dwelling of many there is quarrel; even of two, talk/noise).

statements.claim: The arrow-maker sat straightening and smoothing a shaft with his whole attention, and a king's procession passed on the road behind him with music and banners — it was said the king himself rode in it — and the man never saw it.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'like the arrow-maker so absorbed in straightening his shaft that he did not see the king pass by, the mind should be fixed on one point' (BP 11.9.10-12); the procession details are connective elaboration.

statements.claim: From that man the avadhuta learned to fix his own mind on a single point until nothing could pull it away — such absorption is the whole of the mind kept in one place, not laziness or dreaming.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.10-12 (mana ekatra saṃyuñjyāj jita-śvāso jitāsanaḥ ... ātmany avaruddha-citto na veda kiñcid bahir antaraṃ vā — with the mind thus fixed in the self he knows nothing outside or within); the 'not laziness' gloss is connective.

statements.claim: Solitude and one-pointedness — the maiden's silence and the arrow-maker's absorption — are one discipline: empty the room until nothing clinks, then give the whole mind to the one thing that matters.
statements.evidence: Closing synthesis of the two supported lessons; non-factual framing.

corrections.original_sentence: The birds that took the meat were no stronger in the wing than the osprey — only more numerous, and more hungry.
corrections.suggested: The birds that took the meat were the stronger ones — strong, and hungry, with no prey of their own — and the osprey, burdened by its prize, could not defend it against them.

notes: One CONTRADICTED: BP 11.9.1 (balino 'nye nirāmiṣāḥ) has the attacking birds as the STRONGER ones — the pack index ('seized by stronger birds'), all translations, and the story's own opening agree — but the story later asserts the attackers were 'no stronger in the wing... only more numerous, and more hungry.' Everything else (osprey letting go, honor/disgrace, child, maiden's bangles, arrow-maker) is faithful to BP 11.9.1-12.

statements.claim: The serpent owns nothing — it enters a burrow another creature has abandoned, lies there without care, and moves on homeless; the avadhuta made its way his own, wandering alone and living in no house he had built.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.13 (eka-cāry aniketaḥ syād apramatto guhāśayaḥ — wandering alone, homeless, dwelling in a cave) and pack excerpt ('the serpent enters another's abandoned home and thrives'); the burrow was never its own, so nothing could be taken from it is connective.

statements.claim: Building a house brings only sorrow: the labor of raising the walls, the worry of keeping them, the grief of leaving them — all for a body that will not last.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.14: gṛhārambho hi duḥkhāya viphalaś cādhruvātmanaḥ (undertaking a house is for sorrow, fruitless, for the impermanent self); the labor/worry/grief triad is connective elaboration.

statements.claim: As the spider sends the thread forth from its own heart, plays with it, and draws it back into itself, so the one Lord Narayana — who alone is — spins out the world by his own power, sustains it, and in time withdraws it; the web is not supported by anything outside the spider.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.15-20 (eko nārāyaṇo devaḥ ... sva-māyayā ...; yathorṇanābhir hṛdayād ūrṇāṃ santatya vaktrataḥ) and pack excerpt: 'as the spider sends forth the thread from its own heart, plays with it and draws it back, so the Lord creates, sustains and withdraws the world.'

statements.claim: The wasp takes a living creature and seals it into the mud of a wall; the creature, helpless, broods on the wasp until it becomes like what it contemplates, and in time is a wasp itself.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.22: kīṭaḥ peśaskṛtaṃ dhyāyan kuḍyāṃ tena praveśitaḥ (the insect, meditating on the wasp, is placed by it into the wall) and pack excerpt: 'as the wasp, meditating on its captor, becomes like it.'

statements.claim: So it is with the mind: it becomes what it dwells upon — a mind on the world becomes worldly, a mind on the Lord becomes like the Lord; most men are exactly what they have been thinking of.
statements.evidence: BP 11.9.21-22 (yatra yatra mano dehī dhārayet sakalaṃ dhiyā ... kīṭaḥ peśaskṛtaṃ dhyāyan) and pack excerpt: 'the mind becomes what it dwells upon.' The 'most men... rarely choose' tail is connective.

statements.claim: This was the avadhuta's last and deepest teaching; he had counted twenty-four teachers in all — earth, wind and water, the pigeon and the python, the moth and the bee, the elephant and the deer, the maiden and the arrow-maker — and with the serpent, the spider and the wasp the count was complete.
statements.evidence: The count of twenty-four gurus and the list order (ending in serpent, spider, peśaskṛt) are established in BP 11.7.33-34 (ete me guravo rājan catur-viṃśatir āśritāḥ), quoted in the corpus chain pack DKS_0505; the serpent/spider/wasp are the final three teachers of BP 11.9 (13-22), which closes the avadhuta's enumeration.

statements.claim: All of them, he said, pointed to the same place — past the creatures, to the one who spins them out and draws them back; a strange end to a list that began with the earth underfoot.
statements.evidence: Theistic synthesis consistent with the spider teaching (11.9.15-20) and the corpus arc; non-factual closing framing.

notes: Faithful to BP 11.9.13-22 (serpent's borrowed hole, house-building sorrow, spider/ūrṇanābhi creation-withdrawal, wasp/peśaskṛt meditation). The 'twenty-four teachers... count complete' claim is supported via the corpus chain (DKS_0505 pack, BP 11.7.34 catur-viṃśatir), whose list ends with the serpent, spider and peśaskṛt. No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: Sanaka and his brothers — the mind-born sons of Brahma, the oldest minds in creation — asked Brahma for the subtle goal of yoga; no one, not even their father, could answer.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'The mind-born sons of Brahma asked him the subtle goal of yoga'; index summary: 'unable to get an answer from Brahma, were taught by Krishna himself appearing as a swan.' 'Oldest minds in creation' is connective color consistent with the mind-born Kumaras.

statements.claim: Brahma did not answer from his own knowledge but turned inward and meditated on Krishna; and Krishna, seeing what was needed, appeared before the sages in the form of a swan.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.18 (sa mām acintayad devaḥ praśna-pāra-titīrṣayā — that god, wishing to cross the question, thought of me) and pack excerpt: 'pondering their question, Brahma meditated on me, and I appeared to them in the form of a swan.'

statements.claim: A great white hamsa glided into that assembly; the sages rose, walked up to it, bowed at its feet, and asked who it was that they should be answered by a bird.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.19-20 (dṛṣṭvā mām ta upavrajya kṛtvā pādābhivandanam / ity ahaṃ munibhiḥ pṛṣṭas tattva-jijñāsubhis) and pack excerpt: 'They asked who I was.' The 'that we should be answered by a bird' irony and 'calm as the water it had crossed' are connective.

statements.claim: The swan's reply turned the question back on them: if in truth there is no difference in the self, their question had no ground — know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.21-22 (vastuno yady anānātva ātmanaḥ praśna īdṛśaḥ ...) and pack excerpt: 'if in truth there is no difference in the self, their very question has no ground — know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.'

statements.claim: The mind runs into the qualities of nature and they into it; the more it serves them the deeper it sinks; waking, dreaming and dreamless sleep are only states of the intellect spun out of those qualities.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.24-26: guṇeṣv āviśate ceto guṇāś cetasi ca ... abhīkṣṇaṃ guṇa-sevayā / jāgrat svapnaḥ suṣuptaṃ ca guṇato buddhi-vṛttayaḥ.

statements.claim: Bondage is the self forgetting itself and seeing many where there is one; so long as the sense of difference does not turn back, the knot holds — yet the one who enjoys waking objects, recollects them in dream, and withdraws in deep sleep is the same throughout, the knower behind the senses.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.27-31 (ahaṅkāra-kṛtaṃ bandham ... yāvan nānārtha-dhīḥ puṃso na nivarteta; yo jāgare bahir ... bhuṅkte ... svapne suṣupta upasaṃharate sa ekaḥ ... indriyeśaḥ).

statements.claim: Cut the knot in the heart with the sword of knowledge: the world is the play of the mind, like the circle of fire a whirled burning brand traces — one light, and the eye believes a ring of flame.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.32-33 (sañchidya hārdam ... jñānāsinā; īkṣeta vibhramam idaṃ manaso vilāsaṃ ... alāta-cakram).

statements.claim: Withdraw the gaze, turn from thirst, sit in silence and taste the bliss that is your own self; the body is perishable, put on and taken off like a garment — the awakened man watches the exchange without confusion, as a drunken man hardly notices a change of clothes.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.34-35 (dṛṣṭim pratinivartya nivṛtta-tṛṣṇas tūṣṇīṃ bhaven nija-sukhānubhavo nirīhaḥ; vāso yathā parikṛtaṃ madirā-madāndhaḥ).

statements.claim: Even the body's comings and goings are governed by the acts that set it in motion, and the one established in awareness does not return to the dream once the reality is seen.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.36: deho 'pi daiva-vaśa-gaḥ khalu karma yāvat ... svāpnaṃ punar na bhajate pratibuddha-vastuḥ.

statements.claim: This is the secret of sankhya and yoga, the two great paths; the swan declared: I am the essence of yoga, of sankhya, of truth, of the right, of radiance; all the qualities of nature serve me, who am beyond them, wanting nothing.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.37-39: mayaitad uktaṃ vo viprā guhyaṃ yat sāṅkhya-yogayoḥ / ahaṃ yogasya sāṅkhyasya satyasyartasya tejasaḥ / māṃ bhajanti guṇāḥ sarve nirguṇaṃ nirapekṣakam.

statements.claim: The sages Sanaka and his brothers felt their doubt fall away and worshipped and praised the swan.
statements.evidence: BP 11.13.40-41: iti me chinna-sandehā munayaḥ sanakādayaḥ / tair ahaṃ pūjitaḥ saṃyak saṃstutaḥ paramarṣibhiḥ.

statements.claim: Krishna told all this to Uddhava long afterward; the question the Kumaras had carried dissolved not in an answer but in seeing who it was that asked, and the swan, having done its work, was gone, leaving only the stillness it had pointed to.
statements.evidence: Krishna-to-Uddhava frame is supported (the chapter is Krishna's discourse to Uddhava; pack index: 'Asked by his disciples about the swan form, Krishna recounts...'). The swan's departure is not in the quoted verses (15-41, which end with the Kumaras' worship) — closing connective coda consistent with the appearance-form.

notes: Highly faithful to BP 11.13.15-41: nearly every doctrinal claim maps to its verse (mind-qualities, three states, knot of difference, firebrand circle, withdrawal/bliss, garment body, karma-governed body, sankhya-yoga secret, essence of yoga/sankhya/truth/right/radiance, doubt cut, worship). The closing 'swan was gone' and scene touches are connective; no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: In the city of Avanti lived a brahmin who owned more than anyone and gave away less than anyone; his wealth was a hoard kept like a yaksha's treasure, and his relatives and guests were not honored even with a word; he was miserly by habit and cruel in manner, and his sons and kinsmen turned against him.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.5-8: avantiṣu dvijaḥ kaścid āsīd āḍhyatamaḥ śriyā (a brahmin richest in wealth); vāṅ-mātreṇāpi nārcitāḥ (not honored even with a word); duhśīlasya kadaryasya druhyante putra-bāndhavāḥ; yakṣa-vittasya.

statements.claim: His relatives took part of his wealth and thieves carried off the rest, and he who had been the richest man in Avanti sat looking at his empty rooms; he had lost both worlds — this one's comforts and the merit the next would have counted, worn away by the contempt he had earned.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.8-10: cyutasyobhaya-lokataḥ / tad-avadhyāna-visrasta-puṇya-skandhasya; jñātyo jagṛhuḥ kiñcit kiñcid dasyavaḥ. 'Sat looking at empty rooms' is connective.

statements.claim: For a long time he brooded over the ruin, then the grief turned and he spoke to himself: what calamity is this, that I tormented myself for nothing?
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.12-13: dhyāyato dīrghaṃ naṣṭa-rāyas ... aho kaṣṭaṃ vṛthātmā me 'nutāpitaḥ.

statements.claim: Wealth never gives happiness to a miser — not once, not ever; it brings theft, violence, falsehood, deceit, desire, anger, pride and intoxication — fifteen evils grow from a single root of gold.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.14, 16-18: prāyeṇāthāḥ kadaryāṇāṃ na sukhāya kadācana; steyaṃ hiṃsānṛtaṃ dambhaḥ kāmaḥ krodhaḥ smayo madaḥ / ete pañcadaśānarthā hy artha-mūlā matā nṛṇām.

statements.claim: Brothers break with brothers over the smallest amount; fathers, wives and friends all split apart where money is.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.19-20: bhidyante bhrātaro dārāḥ pitaraḥ suhṛdas tathā / arthenālpīyasā.

statements.claim: He had been given a human birth, which even the immortals pray for, and the highest station of a brahmin — the very door to heaven and to freedom — and spent it chasing a hoard; what use are riches or the givers of riches, desires or the givers of desires?
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.21-26: labdhvā janmāmara-prārthyaṃ mānuṣyaṃ tad dvijāgryatām / svargāpavargayor dvāraṃ ...; kiṃ dhanair dhana-dair vā kiṃ kāmair vā kāma-dair uta.

statements.claim: Surely the Lord Hari, who contains all the gods, is pleased with me, to have stripped all this away; with what life is left I will dry up this body, and the gods of the three worlds will rejoice in me.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.27-29: nūnaṃ me bhagavāṃs tuṣṭaḥ sarva-deva-mayo hariḥ / so 'haṃ kālāvaśeṣeṇa śoṣayiṣye 'ṅgam ātmanaḥ / tatra mām anumoderan devās tri-bhuvaneśvarāḥ.

statements.claim: He left everything, became a silent wandering mendicant with his senses and breath under control, and walked the roads and villages begging his bread.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.31-32: sa cacāra mahīm etāṃ saṃyatātmendriyānilaḥ / taṃ vai pravayasaṃ bhikṣum avadhūtam asaj-janāḥ (he walked the earth, controlled in self, senses and breath; the aged mendicant).

statements.claim: The townspeople tormented him — some snatched his triple staff, some his bowl and water pot, some took the food from his hands on the riverbank; they tried to make the silent man speak and struck him when he would not; they called him a cheat wearing the flag of religion, a fraud; some laughed, some spat insults, and here and there one muttered that he bore it like a mountain.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.32-38: kecit tri-veṇuṃ jagṛhur eke pātraṃ kamaṇḍalum; annaṃ ... bhuñjānasya sarit-taṭe; yata-vācaṃ vācayanti tāḍayanti na vakti cet; eṣa dharma-dhvajaḥ śaṭhaḥ; aho eṣa mahā-sāro dhṛtimān giri-rāḍ iva; vihasanty / durvātayanti.

statements.claim: Mocked and beaten by the base, enduring the pains that come from the world, from the body and from the gods themselves, he lifted his voice and sang a song that has been sung ever since.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.39-41: evaṃ sa bhautikaṃ duḥkhaṃ daivikaṃ daihikaṃ ca yat / paribhūta imāṃ gāthām agāyata narādhamaiḥ. 'A song sung ever since' is connective.

statements.claim: The song: the mind alone creates the qualities of nature and from them all the varied works of men; the self does nothing — it only watches, golden and still, while the mind chases and suffers and calls itself the doer.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.42-43: mano guṇān vai sṛjate ...; anīha ātmā manasā samīhatā hiraṇ-mayo mat-sakha udvicaṣṭe.

statements.claim: For a man whose mind is calm and collected, what need is there of gifts, rites, vows or learning? The gods themselves fell under the mind's sway, and the mind bows to nothing else; it is an unconquerable enemy, unbearable in force, a thorn in the heart, and few master it.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.44-47: samāhitaṃ yasya manaḥ praśāntaṃ dānādibhiḥ kiṃ vada tasya kṛtyam; mano-vaśe 'nye hy abhavan sma devā ...; tam durjayaṃ śatrum asahya-vegam arun-tudaṃ tan na vijitya kecit.

statements.claim: Foolish men look at this body, which is only mind-stuff, and cry I and mine; but neither people, nor gods, nor planets, nor karma, nor time tinges the self with joy or grief — no one outside, anywhere, at any time; the mind alone turns the wheel of existence, and the man who knows this stands on the ground the great seers of old stood on.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.48-56: dehaṃ mano-mātram imaṃ gṛhītvā mamāham ity andha-dhiyo manuṣyāḥ; janas tu hetuḥ ... devatās ... grahā ... karma ... kālaḥ (the five rejected causes); na kenacit kvāpi kathañcanāsya dvandvoparāgaḥ parataḥ parasya; etāṃ ... adhyāsitāṃ pūrvatamair maharṣibhiḥ.

statements.claim: Krishna ended the story with a single sentence: no one gives a person joy or sorrow except his own confusion; therefore, my son, restrain the mind with discernment — with all your strength, restrain it.
statements.evidence: BP 11.23.58-59: sukha-duḥkha-prado nānyaḥ puruṣasyātma-vibhramaḥ / tasmāt sarvātmanā tāta nigṛhāṇa mano dhiyā.

notes: Very faithful to BP 11.23.5-60 — nearly every claim tracks a verse (yaksha-treasure hoard, both worlds lost, fifteen evils from wealth, the five rejected causes of joy/sorrow, Krishna's closing command). No UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: King Pururava, son of Ila (Aila), far-famed and once lord of the whole earth, ran through a forest naked and weeping after the nymph Urvashi, who had left him — mad with grief, unsatisfied, chasing her through years and nights.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.3-5: ailaḥ samrāḍ imāṃ gāthām agāyata bṛhac-chravāḥ / tyaktvātmānaṃ vrayantīṃ tāṃ nagna unmatta-van nṛpaḥ / kāmān atṛpto 'nujuṣan kṣullakān varṣa-yāminīḥ; pack index summary ('pursues her naked and weeping'); name Pururava/Aila per index. Forest setting per index locations.

statements.claim: Krishna told Uddhava this story as a mirror for every man who hands his mind to another and calls it love.
statements.evidence: The story is part of Krishna's discourse to Uddhava (11.26, śrī-bhagavān uvāca frame); the 'mirror held up' purpose is framing.

statements.claim: After long running, in the depth of the forest, the madness broke and he sang the song remembered as the song of Aila: he no longer knew whether the sun had risen or set — he knew only that she was not there.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.3, 7: ailaḥ ... agāyata; nāhaṃ vedābhinirmuktaḥ sūryo vābhyudito 'muyā.

statements.claim: What delusion seized me, that I, a self, made myself the plaything of a woman! I was the lord of the world and threw away my own majesty like a straw to run after her; where is her power, her brilliance, her sovereignty? All of it existed only in my own mind.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.8-10: aho me ātma-sammoho yenātmā yoṣitāṃ kṛtaḥ; sa-paricchadam ātmānaṃ hitvā tṛṇam iveśvaram; kutas tasyānubhāvaḥ syāt teja īśatvam eva vā. 'All of it existed in my own mind' is a connective gloss of the rhetorical question.

statements.claim: What use is learning, austerity, renunciation or scripture to a man who does not know his own good? Shame on me — a fool who thought himself wise; for years I served the nectar of her lips, and the mind she stole from me — what power could have freed it? Even when she spoke well-chosen words to warn me, I was too dull to hear.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.11-15: kiṃ vidyayā kiṃ tapasā kiṃ tyāgena śrutena vā; dhiṅ māṃ mūrkhaṃ paṇḍita-māninam; sevato varṣa-pūgān me urvaśyā adharāsavam; puṃścalyāpahṛtaṃ cittaṃ ko nv anyo mocituṃ prabhuḥ; bodhitasyāpi devyā me sūkta-vākyena durmateḥ.

statements.claim: What harm has she done me? A man sees a snake in a rope and screams — the rope never harmed him; the terror was in the seeing.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.16: kim etayā no 'pakṛtaṃ rajjvā vā sarpa-cetasaḥ.

statements.claim: What is this body I adorned and grieved over — a foul sack of flesh and bone, impure, made of bad smells? Whose is it: my parents', my wife's, my master's, the fire's that will take it, the dogs' and jackals' that will feed on it?
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.17-18: kvāyaṃ malīmasaḥ kāyo daurgandhyādy-ātmako 'śuciḥ; pitroḥ kiṃ svaṃ nu bhāryāyāḥ svāmino 'gneḥ śva-gṛdhrayoḥ.

statements.claim: In this worthless corpse the mind fastens itself, in this heap of skin, flesh, blood, sinew, marrow and bone; let a man who knows his good not cling to women or to anything of the world of women with his senses leashed to desire — attachment is born of contact, of seeing and longing, never from what is unseen and unheard; therefore let there be no contact, no clinging.
statements.evidence: BP 11.26.19-23: tasmin kalevare 'medhye tuccha-niṣṭhe viṣajjate; tvaṅ-māṃsa-rudhira-snāyu-medo-majjāsthi-saṃhatau; athāpi nopasajjeta strīṣu straiṇeṣu cārtha-vit; adṛṣṭād aśrutād bhāvān na bhāva upajāyate; tasmāt saṅgo na kartavyaḥ strīṣu straiṇeṣu cendriyaiḥ.

statements.claim: As he sang, the delusion left him; the emperor who had run naked and weeping rose up clothed in his own understanding, and the peace he had chased settled over him where he stood.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'realizing his delusion, he sings the song of Aila on the futility of attachment to women, and attains peace.' The 'clothed in his own understanding' figure is connective.

statements.claim: Krishna ended the tale: if even Pururava, far-famed lord of the whole earth, was brought so low by a mind fastened on an object of desire, then let anyone who hears the song of Aila look to his own heart.
statements.evidence: The passage closes with the Bhagavan's continuing words (bhp_11.26.025 śrī-bhagavān uvāca in the pack's own text); the moral drawn matches the chapter's purpose in Krishna's instruction to Uddhava.

notes: Faithful to BP 11.26.3-24 (Aila's gāthā: sun-without-her, plaything of a woman, straw-cast majesty, useless learning, body's foul constituents, rope-snake, no-contact doctrine, peace attained). Glosses are connective; no UNSUPPORTED or CONTRADICTED.

statements.claim: The final teaching had been given — the long instruction of the Uddhava Gita, spoken by Krishna to Uddhava in Dwaraka — and now Krishna commanded: Go to my hermitage called Badari, far in the north, by the celestial route, as the blessed go.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.40-43 (Krishna's command to Uddhava; pack excerpt: 'Go, Uddhava, as I have commanded, to my hermitage called Badari'); Vishnu Purana 5.37: 'Do you go by a celestial route... to the holy place Badarikāśrama.' Dwaraka setting per pack index locations.

statements.claim: He was to go to the hermitage on the bank of the Alakananda, where the very sight of the river washes away every stain; there, in the solitude sanctified by the long austerities of Narayana and Nara, patient with the pairs of opposites, gentle in conduct, senses under control, he should abide in the teaching; meditating on Krishna he would come to him beyond the three paths.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.41-43: īkṣayālakanandāyā vidhūtāśeṣa-kalmaṣaḥ / titikṣur dvandva-mātrāṇāṃ suśīlaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ / matto 'nuśikṣitaṃ yat te viviktam anubhāvayan; pack excerpt ('you will come to me beyond the three paths'); VP 5.37 (the spot sanctified by Narayana and Nara; meditating, he obtains perfection).

statements.claim: Uddhava heard the command and could not move — separation from Krishna was the one thing his heart refused, and the friend who had been trusted with more than any other man in Dwaraka stood stricken, unable to leave him.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.45: su-dustyaja-sneha-viyoga-kātaro na śaknuvaṃs taṃ parihātum āturaḥ (tormented by separation from hard-to-give-up affection, unable to leave him). Uddhava's unmatched trust is established through the whole arc (Krishna's final instruction to him, BP 11.6-11.29; corpus DKS_0501-0504).

statements.claim: Uddhava was 'the friend who had carried messages between Krishna and the Pandavas.'
statements.evidence: Characterization padding: Uddhava's role as Krishna's trusted emissary is well established (he delivered Krishna's message to the gopis of Vrindavan, BP 10.46 / corpus DKS_0110-0111, and moved in Krishna's party to Indraprastha, DKS_0371), but no message-carrying specifically between Krishna and the Pandavas appears in this pack or the corpus chain; not contradicted, treated as connective biography.

statements.claim: He walked around Krishna again and again, then knelt, took Krishna's feet and placed them on his own head — and, bearing Krishna's sandals in his hands, went forth.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 11.29.40-45 rendering): 'Uddhava, unable to leave him, walked around him again and again, placed Krishna's feet on his head, and, bearing his sandals, at last went forth.'

statements.claim: He placed the Lord within his own heart and set his face north.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.46: tatas tam antar hṛdi sanniveśya gato mahā-bhāgavato viśālām (the great devotee, placing him within his heart, went to Viśālā [the Badari region, in the north]).

statements.claim: On the way he paused at Hastinapura, where Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him.
statements.evidence: No support in the pack (BP 11.29.40-47, BP 3.4.19-21, VP 5.37, MBh 16.3) for a stop at Hastinapura: the pack's index summary for this story has Uddhava departing directly for Badari (locations: 'Dwaraka, the road to Badarikashrama'), the Vidura-Uddhava dialogue from which BP 3.4.19-21 is drawn took place on the bank of the Yamuna (SB 3.1-3.4; corpus's own account of that meeting, DKS_0527, BP 3.2.1-20, places it on the Yamuna bank after the news of Prabhasa), and the pack's MBh 16.3 instead has Uddhava's leave-taking with the Pandavas at the sea-coast. The place and the mid-journey 'pause' framing are invented.

statements.claim: The story Vidura drew from him — how Uddhava had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, learned the path of self-knowledge, bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and would go on to the hermitage of Badari where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities.
statements.evidence: BP 3.4.19-21 (pack excerpt): 'having worshipped his feet and received the path of self-knowledge, I bowed to the Lord and came away, heart-torn with separation; I will go to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and Nara performed their long austerities.'

statements.claim: Then Uddhava went on, north along the road that climbs toward the mountains, carrying Krishna's sandals and the teaching; Dwaraka and the life he had known there fell behind him.
statements.evidence: BP 11.29.46 (going to Viśālā with Krishna placed in his heart) and the pack's sandals detail; Badari lies north in the Himalayas (VP 5.37). Journey color is connective.

statements.claim: They say the road was long and the hermitage was high, and the man who walked it had left behind himself — the self that clings and grieves — until the walking itself became the teaching.
statements.evidence: Closing devotional reflection; no sourceable factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: On the way he paused at Hastinapura, where Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him: how he had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, how he had learned the path of self-knowledge, how he had bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and how he would go on to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities.
corrections.suggested: And Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him: how he had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, how he had learned the path of self-knowledge, how he had bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and how he would go on to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities.

notes: One UNSUPPORTED: the 'paused at Hastinapura' stop. The pack (11.29.40-47, VP 5.37, MBh 16.3) has Uddhava depart directly for Badari; the Vidura dialogue quoted from BP 3.4.19-21 belongs to the Yamuna-bank meeting (SB 3.1-3.4, per corpus DKS_0527), and MBh 16.3 places Uddhava's leave-taking with the Pandavas at the sea-coast — no source puts him at Hastinapura. Correction drops the location/timing claim while keeping the BP 3.4.19-21 content (Vidura asking, Uddhava telling of the farewell and his Badari plan). The 'carried messages between Krishna and the Pandavas' clause is connective biography (his messenger role to the gopis and presence in the Pandava wedding party are corpus facts).
